prompt: Why can I not point an A record at the IP address of the load balancer?
ten_second: Because those IP addresses change when the load balancer scales. An alias record names the load balancer, and Amazon Route 53 follows the changes.
sixty_second: The short answer is: those IP addresses change, so a fixed A record breaks.
It works like this. As traffic changes, Elastic Load Balancing scales the load balancer.
Then it updates the DNS entry, so the IP addresses can move.
An alias record points to the load balancer itself, not to an address.
Amazon Route 53 detects changes in the load balancer on its own.
So the answers hold the new addresses, and you change nothing.
An alias record also works at callvale.example, where a CNAME record is not allowed.
The thing to watch is customers who want fixed addresses for their firewalls.
An Application Load Balancer has no static addresses. A Network Load Balancer can have them.
In your case, callvale.example and app.callvale.example become alias records to your AWS resources.

follow_ups.question: Which TTL does the alias record use?
follow_ups.answer: You cannot set it. If an alias record points to an AWS resource, Route 53 uses the default TTL for the resource.

prompt: Latency routing or geolocation routing: which one sends my users to the fastest Region?
persona: a SaaS founder in office hours
ten_second: Latency routing. It sends each user to the Region with the best latency. Geolocation routing decides by the user's location, not by speed.
sixty_second: Both choose a Region for each user.
The difference is the goal: speed, or a fixed place for each location.
It works like this. Latency routing uses latency data between users and AWS data centers.
Amazon Route 53 then sends each user to the Region with the best latency.
Geolocation routing looks at where the DNS query comes from.
It matches that location to the records you create.
Location is sometimes a good guide to speed, and sometimes it is not.
The thing to watch is the default record in geolocation routing.
Without a default record, users from other locations get no answer.
In your case, use latency routing if speed is the goal.
Use geolocation routing when a rule keeps one country's users in one Region.

follow_ups.question: And what is geoproximity routing?
follow_ups.answer: Geoproximity routing uses the location of your resources. You can set a bias, which expands or shrinks the geographic region from which traffic goes to a resource.

follow_ups.question: Can latency routing still send users to a Region that is down?
follow_ups.answer: Not if you associate a health check with each record. If a health check finds the resource unhealthy, Route 53 routes traffic away from the associated record.

prompt: We run in two Regions. If the first Region fails, how does DNS move our users to the second one, and how fast?
ten_second: Use failover records with a health check on the primary. Users move after the checks fail and their cached answer expires.
sixty_second: The short answer is: failover records, with a health check on the primary Region.
It works like this. You create a primary record and a secondary record.
Health checkers test the primary endpoint at a regular interval.
By default, three failed checks in a row make the primary unhealthy.
Then Amazon Route 53 answers with the secondary record instead.
But resolvers keep the old answer until its TTL runs out.
So keep that TTL at a minute or less.
The thing to watch is your recovery path.
Create the records and health checks in advance. Don't plan to edit records during the outage.
If seconds matter, look at AWS Global Accelerator: its changes propagate in seconds.
In your case, point each record to the load balancer in that Region.

follow_ups.answer: No. Create an alias record that points to the load balancer and set Evaluate Target Health to true.

follow_ups.question: What happens if both Regions fail their health checks?
follow_ups.answer: Route 53 still answers. If none of the records in a group are healthy, Route 53 considers all of them healthy and selects one based on the routing policy.

prompt: Our domain is registered with another company. Do we have to move it to AWS to use Route 53?
persona: a startup founder in office hours
ten_second: No. You keep the registration where it is. You create a hosted zone, and your registrar points the domain to the zone's name servers.
sixty_second: The short answer is no: you can keep the domain at your registrar.
It works like this. You create a public hosted zone in Amazon Route 53.
You copy your DNS records into that hosted zone.
Amazon Route 53 gives the hosted zone a unique set of four name servers.
At your registrar, you replace the old name servers with those four.
After that, resolvers ask Amazon Route 53 for your records.
The thing to watch is caching during the switch.
Resolvers remember the old name servers for some time.
So first lower the TTL of the NS record at both DNS providers.
If something is missing, you can then go back with less downtime.
In your case, check that every record is in the hosted zone before the switch.
